options.why_wrong: ignores that a virtual image still forms, located by extending the diverging rays backwards.

options.text: A real image, but only if the object is also exactly at the focal point.
options.why_wrong: confuses the special case of the object at the focal point (where no clear image forms at a finite distance) with the general within-f case, which gives a virtual image.

mcq.explanation: An object within the focal length always produces a virtual, upright, magnified image, located where the backward extensions of the two rays cross.

mcq.stem: A student draws one principal ray correctly from an object through a converging lens and marks a point on that ray as 'the image'. What is wrong with this method?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, provided the one ray obeys the correct principal-ray rule.
options.why_wrong: ignores that a single ray only shows one possible path, not a unique crossing point.

options.text: One ray alone cannot identify a unique image point; a second ray (or its extension) is needed to find where they cross.
The image can only be found using the ray through the centre of the lens, never the ray parallel to the axis.
options.why_wrong: wrongly favours one rule over the other; both rays are needed together, regardless of which rule each follows.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, as long as the point chosen lies exactly on the axis.
options.why_wrong: invents an unrelated condition (lying on the axis) that has nothing to do with correctly locating an image.

mcq.explanation: An image is only located where two rays from the same object point (or their backward extensions) actually cross; one ray alone is never enough.

mcq.stem: Which statement correctly compares red and violet light in the visible spectrum?

options.text: Red has the higher frequency and the shorter wavelength.
options.why_wrong: reverses both quantities: red actually has the lower frequency and the longer wavelength.

options.text: Violet has the higher frequency but the longer wavelength.
options.why_wrong: gets frequency right but wrongly pairs it with a longer wavelength; higher frequency always means shorter wavelength here, since c=fλ is fixed.

options.text: Violet has the higher frequency and the shorter wavelength.
Red and violet have the same frequency, but different wavelengths.
options.why_wrong: wrongly treats the two colours as sharing a frequency; different colours are, by definition, different frequencies (and wavelengths).

mcq.explanation: Violet has the highest frequency and shortest wavelength of the visible colours; red has the lowest frequency and longest wavelength.

mcq.stem: A converging lens has focal length $f$. An object is placed exactly at $2f$ from the lens. What best describes the resulting real image?

options.text: Magnified, at a distance greater than $2f$.
options.why_wrong: describes the case for an object placed between f and 2f, not exactly at 2f.

options.text: Diminished, at a distance less than $f$.
options.why_wrong: describes neither the 2f case nor any valid real-image case for a converging lens; a real image never forms closer than f.

options.text: Virtual, at a distance of $2f$ on the same side as the object.
options.why_wrong: wrongly calls a real-image case virtual; an object at 2f, being beyond f, always gives a real image.

options.text: The same size as the object, at a distance of $2f$ on the far side of the lens.

mcq.explanation: An object exactly at $2f$ always gives a real, inverted image of exactly the same size, at $2f$ on the far side of the lens.

flashcards.front: What is the principal focus of a converging lens?
flashcards.back: The point on the axis where rays travelling parallel to the axis converge after passing through the lens; its distance from the lens is the focal length.

flashcards.front: State the two principal-ray rules used to construct a lens image.
flashcards.back: A ray parallel to the axis refracts through the far focus; a ray through the centre of the lens continues undeviated.

flashcards.front: Does a converging lens always produce a real image?
flashcards.back: No. Only when the object is beyond the focal length. Within the focal length, it produces a virtual, upright, magnified image instead, as in a magnifying glass.

flashcards.front: Compare a real lens image with a virtual lens image.
flashcards.back: Real: object beyond f, image on the far side where rays actually cross, inverted. Virtual: object within f, image on the near side where backward extensions cross, upright and magnified.

flashcards.front: In order of increasing frequency, what are the seven colours a prism produces from white light?
flashcards.back: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet (the same order as increasing bending by the prism, and decreasing wavelength).

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Every object placed in front of a converging lens produces a real image.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Most introductory examples use an object placed well beyond the lens, where a real image does form, so that case can be mistaken for the only possible outcome.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner tries to construct a real image (two converging rays meeting on the far side of the lens) for an object placed closer to the lens than its focal length.
misconceptions.correct_model: A converging lens only produces a real image when the object is further from the lens than the focal length. When the object is within the focal length, the two rays leaving the lens diverge and never meet on the far side; only their backward extensions meet, on the same side as the object, giving a virtual, magnified image, as in a magnifying glass.
misconceptions.remediation: Before constructing any lens diagram, compare the object's distance with the focal length first, and predict whether a real or virtual image is even possible before drawing a single ray.
related_exercises: the object-position classification exercise in this lesson

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A single ray is enough to determine where a lens image forms.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: One ray is often drawn first while explaining the rule it follows, which can look like it has already 'found' the image, before a second ray is added.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner marks an image point as soon as one ray is drawn, rather than waiting for a second ray (or its extension) to cross it.
misconceptions.correct_model: A single ray only shows one possible path light could take from the object through the lens; it does not by itself pin down a unique point. The image is located only where two rays from the same object point (or their backward extensions) actually cross.
misconceptions.remediation: Always draw both principal rays before marking any image point, and check explicitly that they cross (or that their extensions cross) at the point being marked.
related_exercises: every two-ray construction in this lesson's theory

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Red light has a higher frequency than violet light.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Red is often associated with 'high energy' warnings (heat, danger) in everyday language, which can be wrongly carried over into assuming it also means higher frequency.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner orders the visible spectrum with red at the high-frequency end instead of violet.
misconceptions.correct_model: Violet light has the highest frequency and shortest wavelength in the visible spectrum; red light has the lowest frequency and longest wavelength. Frequency and wavelength always run in opposite order across the visible spectrum, since their product is the constant speed of light.
misconceptions.remediation: Use $c=f\lambda$ with a fixed $c$: since violet's wavelength is the shortest of the visible colours, its frequency must be the highest, and the reverse for red.
related_exercises: the colour-ordering exercise in this lesson

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a converging lens always produces a real image.
common_mistakes.why: The most familiar early examples (a magnifying glass used to focus sunlight, a camera) tend to use an object well beyond the focal length.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Compare the object's distance with the focal length before constructing anything: beyond f gives real; within f gives virtual.

common_mistakes.mistake: Marking an image point after drawing only one principal ray.
common_mistakes.why: One ray, drawn correctly, can look like it has already 'found' the image before a second ray is added.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always draw both principal rays (or both their backward extensions) and mark the image only where they actually cross.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ordering the visible spectrum with red at the high-frequency end.
common_mistakes.why: Everyday language links red with 'hot' or 'intense', which can be wrongly carried over into frequency.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Use c = fλ with fixed c: violet, having the shortest wavelength, must have the highest frequency, and red the lowest.

exam_notes: State explicitly whether an image is real or virtual before describing its other properties; this is usually a separate, required statement in the mark scheme.
Always construct (or describe) both principal rays; an answer based on only one ray rarely earns full marks, even if that ray is correctly drawn.
When ordering spectrum colours, give the order consistently as either 'by increasing frequency' or 'by increasing wavelength', and never mix the two directions in the same list.

summary.big_idea: A converging lens images an object using two principal rays, giving a real, inverted image when the object is beyond the focal length and a virtual, enlarged image when it is within it, while a prism disperses white light into a fixed colour order running opposite to wavelength.
key_points: A ray parallel to the axis refracts through the far focus; a ray through the lens centre is undeviated; the image is only where two such rays (or their extensions) cross.
Object beyond f: real, inverted image, diminished beyond 2f, enlarged between f and 2f, same size exactly at 2f.
Object within f: virtual, upright, enlarged image on the object's side, found by extending both rays backwards, as in a magnifying glass.
A prism disperses white light into red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet, in order of increasing frequency and decreasing wavelength, with violet bent the most.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Compare the object's distance with f first (real if beyond, virtual if within), always use two rays to find the image, and remember violet bends most and has the highest frequency, red the least and the lowest.

06_The_electromagnetic_spectrum.json.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
06_The_electromagnetic_spectrum.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Order the seven regions of the electromagnetic spectrum by frequency and wavelength, state that all travel at the same speed in a vacuum, and match each region to a named use and an excessive-exposure harm where relevant.

Recall that the speed of electromagnetic waves in a vacuum (and approximately in air) is about 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, and use it with v = fλ to calculate the frequency or wavelength of an electromagnetic wave.

prerequisites.statement: Use the wave equation v = fλ to relate wave speed, frequency and wavelength, from earlier in this unit.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The electromagnetic spectrum is simply a family of waves sharing one speed in vacuum, ordered by frequency and wavelength using exactly this equation.

prerequisites.statement: Recall the visible spectrum's colour order (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet) from the previous lesson.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Visible light is one region of the electromagnetic spectrum; its colour order is simply a closer look at one small part of the ordering this lesson extends to the whole spectrum.

diagnostic_items.question: An ultrasound wave travels through water at 1500 m/s with a wavelength of 0.25 m. What is its frequency?

common_wrong_answers.answer: 375 Hz
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner multiplies speed by wavelength instead of dividing, using $v = f\lambda$ without first rearranging it for the quantity actually asked for.
The learner divides the wavelength by the speed, inverting the correct ratio; the unit check fails, because metres divided by metres per second gives seconds, not hertz.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Every calculation in this lesson is $c = f\lambda$ with the speed fixed at $3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so the equation has to be safe to rearrange for either frequency or wavelength before the large numbers are added.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write $v = f\lambda$, circle the unknown and rearrange on paper before substituting, then check the unit of the answer: m/s divided by m leaves $1/\mathrm{s}$, which is Hz.

diagnostic_items.question: List the seven colours of the visible spectrum in order, starting with the longest wavelength and ending with the shortest. Which end of your list has the highest frequency?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. The violet end has the highest frequency, because frequency rises as wavelength falls.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner knows the sequence but gives it in order of increasing wavelength, so the two ends of the spectrum are the wrong way round.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet, with red having the highest frequency
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The order is right, but the learner pairs the longest wavelength with the highest frequency, treating the two quantities as rising together instead of inversely.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This lesson orders the whole spectrum by frequency and by wavelength, with visible light as one narrow region whose own colour order runs the same way; a student with red and violet reversed will also place radio waves and gamma rays the wrong way round.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Learn the order once, red to violet, and attach a single fact to it: red has the longest wavelength and the lowest frequency of the seven. Then check for every pair you name that a longer wavelength goes with a lower frequency.

theory_blocks.title: One family of waves, from radio to gamma rays
theory_blocks.body: Radio waves carrying a broadcast, the visible light you see this page by, and the X-rays used at a dentist's surgery seem like completely different things. In fact, they are all the same fundamental kind of wave: a transverse wave that, unlike sound, does not need any material medium to travel through, and can travel through a vacuum. What distinguishes radio from visible light from X-rays is simply their **frequency** (and correspondingly, their **wavelength**): together, they form one continuous family called the [[blue:**electromagnetic spectrum**]].

theory_blocks.title: Seven regions, one shared speed in vacuum
theory_blocks.body:
The electromagnetic spectrum is divided, by convention, into seven named regions, listed here in order of **increasing frequency** (and correspondingly, decreasing wavelength):

$$\text{radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma}$$

There are no sharp edges between neighbouring regions: the boundaries are a matter of convention, not a sudden change in the physics. What never changes across the whole spectrum is this: **every** electromagnetic wave travels at the same speed in a vacuum, whatever its frequency or wavelength. A radio wave and a gamma ray differ enormously in frequency and wavelength, but not in how fast they travel through empty space.

assets.caption: The seven regions of the electromagnetic spectrum, in order of increasing frequency from left to right, and so decreasing wavelength from left to right: the two arrows point in opposite directions along the same, continuous spectrum.
assets.purpose: Make the opposite-direction relationship between frequency and wavelength (the source of the related idea) directly visible on the full seven-region ordering.

theory_blocks.title: Matching each region to its uses
theory_blocks.body:
Each region's typical uses follow from how strongly it is absorbed, reflected or detected by different materials:

- **Radio**: broadcasting (television and radio transmission) and radar.
- **Microwave**: satellite communication, mobile phone signals, and microwave ovens (absorbed strongly by water molecules in food).
- **Infrared**: remote controls, and thermal imaging (detecting heat given off by warm objects).
- **Visible**: human vision, and photography.
- **Ultraviolet**: detecting forged bank notes (genuine notes carry a UV-sensitive marking), among other uses.
- **X-ray**: medical imaging (seeing bone through soft tissue) and airport security scanning.
- **Gamma**: detecting and treating cancer (destroying or imaging cancerous cells).

theory_blocks.title: Not every region is equally hazardous
theory_blocks.body: Being described as 'electromagnetic' does not, by itself, tell you how hazardous a wave is: that depends on the specific region and the amount of exposure. **Excessive** ultraviolet exposure can damage skin cells (sunburn, and a longer-term increased skin cancer risk) and eyes; **excessive** X-ray or gamma exposure can mutate or damage cells more deeply, which is why medical and security X-ray use is kept to the minimum needed, and why gamma sources are carefully shielded and controlled. Radio waves and microwaves, at the exposure levels found in ordinary use (broadcasting, phone signals, a correctly sealed microwave oven), are not associated with this kind of cell damage. The key word throughout is [[red:**excessive**]]: moderate, ordinary exposure to most regions carries little or no such risk, while uncontrolled exposure to the higher-frequency regions does.

theory_blocks.title: The speed of light, and using c = fλ
theory_blocks.body:
The shared speed of all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum has the symbol $c$, and its value is:
$$c \approx 3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$$
This is also, to a very good approximation, the speed of electromagnetic waves in air. Because this is just the ordinary wave equation with a fixed speed, $c=f\lambda$ can be rearranged exactly as in earlier lessons to find a frequency or wavelength: for a radio station broadcasting at $f=100\,\mathrm{MHz}=1.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, $\lambda=c/f=(3.0\times10^{8})/(1.0\times10^{8})=3.0\,\mathrm{m}$.

keywords.definition: The continuous family of transverse waves, from radio to gamma rays, that all travel at the same speed in a vacuum and need no medium to travel through.
The shared speed, symbol c, of all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum, approximately 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
The electromagnetic region just beyond violet light in frequency, able to damage skin and eyes with excessive exposure.
A high-frequency electromagnetic region used for medical and security imaging, requiring exposure to be carefully limited.
The highest-frequency, shortest-wavelength region of the electromagnetic spectrum, used in cancer detection and treatment.

worked_examples.statement: **Gamma versus radio.** Compare a gamma ray and a radio wave, both travelling in a vacuum. State which has the higher frequency, which has the shorter wavelength, and which travels faster.
knowns: both waves are electromagnetic, travelling in a vacuum
reasoning: The gamma ray is from the high-frequency end of the spectrum, the radio wave from the low-frequency end.
All electromagnetic waves share the same speed in a vacuum, regardless of frequency or wavelength.
worked_examples.solution: The gamma ray has the higher frequency and the shorter wavelength. Neither travels faster: both travel at exactly the same speed in a vacuum.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the single most important fact about the electromagnetic spectrum to get right: frequency and wavelength vary hugely across it, but speed in vacuum never does.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the gamma ray, being 'more dangerous' or 'higher energy', must also travel faster.

worked_examples.statement: **A radio station's wavelength.** A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of $100\,\mathrm{MHz}$ ($1.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{Hz}$). Calculate its wavelength.
reasoning: Rearrange $c=f\lambda$ to $\lambda=c/f$ and substitute.
worked_examples.solution: $\lambda = (3.0\times10^{8})\div(1.0\times10^{8}) = 3.0\,\mathrm{m}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $f\lambda = (1.0\times10^8)\times3.0 = 3.0\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s} = c$, as required.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting to convert $100\,\mathrm{MHz}$ into $1.0\times10^8\,\mathrm{Hz}$ before substituting, leading to an answer a million times too large.

worked_examples.statement: **A microwave oven's frequency.** A microwave oven produces electromagnetic waves of wavelength $0.122\,\mathrm{m}$. (a) Calculate their frequency. (b) Explain why this calculation does not contradict the idea that all electromagnetic waves share the same speed in vacuum.
reasoning: (a) Rearrange $c=f\lambda$ to $f=c/\lambda$.
(b) Different microwave ovens, or different regions of the spectrum, can have different frequencies and wavelengths while still keeping the product $f\lambda$ fixed at $c$.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $f = (3.0\times10^8)\div0.122 \approx 2.5\times10^9\,\mathrm{Hz}$ (about $2.5\,\mathrm{GHz}$). (b) The calculation only finds this particular wave's own frequency and wavelength; it does not change the fact that $f\lambda$ still equals the same fixed $c$ for this wave, just as it does for every other electromagnetic wave.
worked_examples.interpretation: A different frequency and a different wavelength are two sides of the same fixed-speed relationship, not evidence of a different speed.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Treating a calculated frequency that differs from another wave's frequency as evidence that the two waves must also travel at different speeds.

worked_examples.statement: **X-rays at the hospital.** A hospital X-ray machine produces electromagnetic waves of wavelength $1.0\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m}$. (a) Calculate their frequency. (b) State one medical use of X-rays. (c) State one precaution taken to reduce the risk from excessive X-ray exposure.
reasoning: (a) Use $f=c/\lambda$.
(b)-(c) Recall this region's standard use and the exposure-limiting precaution associated with it.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $f = (3.0\times10^8)\div(1.0\times10^{-10}) = 3.0\times10^{18}\,\mathrm{Hz}$. (b) Medical imaging, for example to see broken bones through soft tissue. (c) Keeping the X-ray dose, and the number of scans, to the minimum needed, and shielding staff and other patients from the beam (for example, with a lead apron or by leaving the room during the scan).
worked_examples.interpretation: The huge frequency found in part (a), compared with the radio and microwave examples earlier, is a useful check that X-rays really do sit at the high-frequency end of the spectrum.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Giving a general statement like 'X-rays are dangerous' for part (c) instead of a specific, named precaution.

guided_exercises.statement: Put these four regions in order of increasing frequency: ultraviolet, microwave, gamma, infrared.
hints: Recall the full seven-region order: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
Pick out just these four regions from that full order, keeping their relative order.
The lowest-frequency region of these four comes first.
common_errors: Placing gamma first, by associating 'most dangerous' with 'comes first' rather than with 'highest frequency'.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Recall the full seven-region order: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

**Step 2 — Method:** Pick out just these four regions from that full order, keeping their relative order.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Microwave, infrared, ultraviolet, gamma.

**Step 4 — Check:** The lowest-frequency region of these four comes first.

guided_exercises.statement: An AM radio signal has a frequency of $3.0\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{Hz}$. Calculate its wavelength.
hints: Use $\lambda=c/f$ with $c=3.0\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
Divide carefully, keeping track of the powers of ten.
Check your answer is a sensible size for a radio wavelength (metres, not millimetres or kilometres).
common_errors: Mishandling the powers of ten and getting an answer far too large or too small to be a sensible radio wavelength.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Use $\lambda=c/f$ with $c=3.0\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

**Step 2 — Method:** Divide carefully, keeping track of the powers of ten.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $\lambda = (3.0\times10^8)\div(3.0\times10^6) = 1.0\times10^2 = 100\,\mathrm{m}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your answer is a sensible size for a radio wavelength (metres, not millimetres or kilometres).

exercises.statement: Match each use to the correct region of the electromagnetic spectrum: (a) radar; (b) detecting a forged bank note; (c) a television remote control; (d) treating cancer.
exercises.answer: (a) Radio. (b) Ultraviolet. (c) Infrared. (d) Gamma.
exercises.full_solution: Each use follows from how that region specifically interacts with materials: radar reflects off distant objects, UV markings fluoresce, infrared is detected by a remote's receiver, and gamma can destroy cancerous cells.

exercises.statement: Explain why excessive ultraviolet exposure is considered hazardous, while ordinary exposure to visible light is not, even though both are regions of the same electromagnetic spectrum.
exercises.answer: Ultraviolet has a higher frequency (and more energy per wave) than visible light, and excessive exposure to it can damage skin cells and eyes, with a longer-term increased skin cancer risk. Visible light, at ordinary exposure levels, is not associated with this kind of cell damage; sharing the label 'electromagnetic' does not mean sharing the same level of hazard.
exercises.full_solution: The two regions differ specifically in frequency, which is what changes the interaction with living tissue, not in anything else that 'electromagnetic' implies by itself.

exercises.statement: Visible light of wavelength $500\,\mathrm{nm}$ ($5.0\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}$) travels through a vacuum. Calculate its frequency.
exercises.answer: $f = c/\lambda = (3.0\times10^8)\div(5.0\times10^{-7}) = 6.0\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $f\lambda = (6.0\times10^{14})\times(5.0\times10^{-7}) = 3.0\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s} = c$, as required.

exercises.statement: Using the general wave equation idea from earlier in this unit, explain why every electromagnetic wave, whatever its frequency, must have a correspondingly adjusted wavelength, given that they all share the same fixed speed in a vacuum.
exercises.answer: As with any wave obeying $v=f\lambda$, if the speed $v$ is fixed, then frequency and wavelength cannot vary independently: whenever one increases, the other must decrease by the same factor, so that their product stays equal to the fixed speed. For electromagnetic waves, this fixed speed is $c$, so every change in frequency across the spectrum forces a corresponding, opposite change in wavelength.
exercises.full_solution: This is exactly the same v = fλ reasoning used for water waves and sound earlier in this unit, now applied to the special case where the speed is fixed for every member of the family (vacuum), rather than only fixed within one medium at a time.

exam_questions.statement: An electromagnetic wave has a frequency of $1.0\times10^{9}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ ($1.0\,\mathrm{GHz}$). (a) Calculate its wavelength. (b) State which region of the electromagnetic spectrum this wave most likely belongs to, giving a reason.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\lambda = (3.0\times10^8)\div(1.0\times10^9) = 0.30\,\mathrm{m}$. (b) Microwave: a wavelength of a few tens of centimetres is typical of the microwave region, used for example in mobile phone and satellite signals.
exam_questions.full_solution: Comparing a calculated wavelength against the typical scale of each named region is a standard way to identify which region an unfamiliar frequency belongs to.
mark_scheme: Calculates $\lambda=0.30\,\mathrm{m}$.
Identifies the region as microwave.
Gives a reason linking the wavelength scale to that region.
Shows correct rearrangement of $c=f\lambda$ ($\lambda=c/f$).
common_errors: Misplacing a power of ten in the division, giving a wavelength scale that does not match any sensible named region.

exam_questions.statement: A hospital uses one type of electromagnetic radiation to image a patient's broken bone, and a different type to treat a patient's internal tumour. (a) Identify the most likely region of the spectrum used for each purpose. (b) State one safety precaution associated with each.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Imaging the bone: X-ray. Treating the tumour: gamma. (b) X-ray: keeping the dose and number of scans to the minimum needed, and shielding those not being scanned. Gamma: shielding the radioactive source carefully and controlling the treatment dose and exposure time precisely.
exam_questions.full_solution: Both regions are high-frequency and carry excessive-exposure risks, which is exactly why each use comes with a specific, named precaution rather than being treated as automatically safe.
mark_scheme: Identifies X-ray for bone imaging.
Identifies gamma for tumour treatment.
States a specific precaution for X-ray use.
States a specific precaution for gamma use.
common_errors: Swapping the two regions (using gamma for imaging and X-ray for treatment), the reverse of their standard medical uses.

challenge_questions.statement: A ground station sends television signals up to a satellite $3.6\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m}$ above it, and the satellite sends them straight back down to a receiver beside the ground station. Take the speed of electromagnetic waves to be $3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$. (a) Calculate the shortest possible time between a signal leaving the ground station and the same signal reaching the receiver, and say what a viewer would notice. (b) The uplink uses a frequency of $14\,\mathrm{GHz}$, that is $1.4\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{Hz}$; calculate its wavelength. (c) A second channel uses a wavelength of $0.075\,\mathrm{m}$; calculate its frequency and state which of the two channels lies nearer the radio end of the electromagnetic spectrum. (d) Explain why no change to the transmitter could make the delay in part (a) any shorter.
hints: The signal makes a round trip: up to the satellite and then down again.
Use $c = f\lambda$, rearranged for the quantity you need, and keep everything in metres and seconds.
For part (d), ask which quantity in $c = f\lambda$ is the same for every electromagnetic wave in a vacuum.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) The signal travels up and then down, a total distance of $2\times3.6\times10^{7} = 7.2\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m}$, so $t = d/c = (7.2\times10^{7})/(3.0\times10^{8}) = 0.24\,\mathrm{s}$. A viewer would notice a short but real delay of about a quarter of a second, which is why a presenter interviewing someone over a satellite link waits awkwardly before each reply. (b) $\lambda = c/f = (3.0\times10^{8})/(1.4\times10^{10}) = 2.1\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}$, about 2.1 cm, which is a microwave. (c) $f = c/\lambda = (3.0\times10^{8})/0.075 = 4.0\times10^{9}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, that is $4.0\,\mathrm{GHz}$. This is the lower frequency and the longer wavelength of the two, so this channel lies nearer the radio end of the spectrum than the $14\,\mathrm{GHz}$ one. (d) Every electromagnetic wave travels at the same speed in a vacuum, whatever its frequency or wavelength, so changing the frequency, the aerial or the transmitter power cannot make the signal travel any faster. The only way to shorten the delay would be to shorten the path, and the satellite's height is fixed by the orbit it has to keep.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Each part uses one of the lesson's two ideas - a single shared speed, and $c = f\lambda$ - but part (a) asks the student to turn a distance and a speed into something a person would actually experience, and part (d) tests whether 'all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum' has been understood as a limit on what engineering can do, rather than as a sentence to recall.

mcq.stem: A radio wave and a gamma ray both travel through a vacuum. Which statement is correct?

options.text: They travel at the same speed, but the gamma ray has a much higher frequency.
The gamma ray travels faster, because it has a much higher frequency.
options.why_wrong: wrongly links a higher frequency with a higher speed; speed in vacuum is the same for every electromagnetic wave.

options.text: The radio wave travels faster, because it has a much longer wavelength.
options.why_wrong: wrongly links a longer wavelength with a higher speed; again, speed in vacuum does not depend on wavelength.

options.text: Neither can be compared, because they are fundamentally different kinds of wave.
options.why_wrong: wrongly denies that radio waves and gamma rays belong to the same family of electromagnetic waves.

mcq.explanation: All electromagnetic waves share the same speed in a vacuum; only their frequency and wavelength differ, and here the gamma ray has the much higher frequency.

mcq.stem: Which statement about hazards across the electromagnetic spectrum is correct?

options.text: Every region of the spectrum carries an equal risk of cell damage for the same exposure.
options.why_wrong: ignores that hazard depends on the specific region (and its frequency), not on simply being electromagnetic.

options.text: Excessive exposure to ultraviolet, X-rays or gamma rays can damage cells; ordinary radio and microwave exposure is not associated with this kind of damage.
Only visible light is hazardous, since it is the only region humans can detect directly.
options.why_wrong: wrongly ties hazard to visibility, when the genuinely hazardous regions (ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma) are not visible at all.

options.text: Radio waves are the most hazardous region, because they are used for long-distance broadcasting.
options.why_wrong: wrongly ties hazard to how widely a region is used, rather than to its frequency and energy.

mcq.explanation: Hazard depends on the specific region: excessive exposure to the higher-frequency regions (ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma) can damage cells, while ordinary radio and microwave exposure is not associated with this.

mcq.stem: As you move along the electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves towards gamma rays, what happens to frequency and wavelength?

options.text: Both frequency and wavelength increase.
options.why_wrong: ignores that frequency and wavelength vary in opposite directions across the spectrum, since their product (a fixed speed) cannot increase.

options.text: Both frequency and wavelength decrease.
options.why_wrong: gets the direction of frequency wrong; frequency increases from radio towards gamma, it does not decrease.

options.text: Frequency increases; wavelength decreases.
Frequency decreases; wavelength increases.
options.why_wrong: reverses both quantities: frequency increases and wavelength decreases from radio towards gamma, not the other way round.

mcq.explanation: Moving from radio towards gamma rays, frequency increases while wavelength decreases, keeping their product equal to the fixed speed in vacuum.

mcq.stem: An electromagnetic wave has a wavelength of $1.5\,\mathrm{m}$. What is its frequency?

options.text: $4.5\times10^8\,\mathrm{Hz}$
options.why_wrong: multiplies $c$ by $\lambda$ instead of dividing, giving units that are not even a valid frequency for this calculation.

options.text: $2.0\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{Hz}$
options.why_wrong: has the right digits but a power-of-ten error, giving an impossibly low frequency.

options.text: $1.5\,\mathrm{Hz}$
options.why_wrong: treats the wavelength value itself as if it were already the frequency, without using c = fλ at all.

options.text: $2.0\times10^8\,\mathrm{Hz}$

mcq.explanation: $f=c/\lambda=(3.0\times10^8)\div1.5=2.0\times10^8\,\mathrm{Hz}$.

flashcards.front: List the seven regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency.
flashcards.back: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

flashcards.front: What is the speed of electromagnetic waves in a vacuum, and what equation links it to frequency and wavelength?
flashcards.back: c ≈ 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s, linked by c = fλ.

flashcards.front: Do gamma rays travel faster than radio waves in a vacuum?
flashcards.back: No. Every electromagnetic wave travels at the same speed in a vacuum; only frequency and wavelength differ between regions.

flashcards.front: Compare the hazard from excessive ultraviolet exposure with the hazard from ordinary radio-wave exposure.
flashcards.back: Excessive ultraviolet exposure can damage skin cells and eyes; ordinary radio-wave exposure is not associated with this kind of cell damage. Hazard depends on the specific region, not on simply being 'electromagnetic'.

flashcards.front: Which region of the electromagnetic spectrum is used for medical imaging of bones, and which for treating cancer internally?
flashcards.back: X-rays for bone imaging; gamma rays for treating cancer.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Gamma rays travel faster than radio waves in a vacuum.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Gamma rays are associated with very high energy and danger, which can be wrongly extended into assuming they also travel faster.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner ranks electromagnetic waves by speed in vacuum, rather than stating that all of them share the same speed there.
misconceptions.correct_model: All electromagnetic waves, from radio to gamma rays, travel at exactly the same speed in a vacuum (about 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s), regardless of their frequency or wavelength. They differ enormously in frequency and wavelength, never in vacuum speed.
misconceptions.remediation: Use v = fλ with a fixed v: since frequency and wavelength vary in opposite directions to keep v constant, no region of the spectrum needs, or gets, a different speed in vacuum.
related_exercises: the gamma-versus-radio comparison in this lesson's first worked example

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Every region of the electromagnetic spectrum is equally dangerous for the same amount of exposure.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: All seven regions share the label 'electromagnetic wave', which can suggest they share the same level of risk as well as the same basic nature.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner treats ordinary visible light exposure as being just as hazardous as excessive ultraviolet, X-ray or gamma exposure, or vice versa, treats radio waves as automatically dangerous.
misconceptions.correct_model: Different regions carry very different amounts of energy and interact with living tissue very differently. Excessive exposure to ultraviolet, X-rays or gamma rays can damage or mutate cells; radio waves and microwaves at ordinary, everyday exposure levels are not associated with this kind of cell damage. Being electromagnetic does not by itself mean equally hazardous.
misconceptions.remediation: Pair each region with its specific, named harm (or 'no significant harm at ordinary exposure') rather than a single blanket statement about danger.
related_exercises: the uses-and-hazards matching exercise in this lesson

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Wavelength and frequency increase together across the electromagnetic spectrum.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both quantities are often introduced as simply 'getting bigger' as you move along the spectrum diagram from left to right, without checking which one is actually increasing in which direction.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner states that gamma rays have both the highest frequency and the longest wavelength, or the equivalent error for radio waves.
misconceptions.correct_model: Across the electromagnetic spectrum, wavelength and frequency vary in opposite directions: moving from radio towards gamma rays, frequency increases while wavelength decreases, because their product (the fixed speed in vacuum) stays the same throughout.
misconceptions.remediation: Always check a stated frequency and wavelength against v = fλ with the fixed speed of light: if both are claimed to increase together, the calculated 'speed' would not stay constant, which is impossible for this family of waves.
related_exercises: the region-ordering guided exercise in this lesson

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a higher-frequency region of the spectrum travels faster in vacuum.
common_mistakes.why: Higher frequency is linked with 'more energy' and 'more dangerous' in everyday language, which can be wrongly carried over into speed.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember v = fλ with a fixed v in vacuum: frequency and wavelength change to keep the product constant; speed itself never changes between regions.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating every region of the spectrum as equally hazardous, or equally safe.
common_mistakes.why: All seven regions share the single label 'electromagnetic', which can suggest they also share the same level of risk.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Pair each region with its own, specific hazard statement (or 'no significant hazard at ordinary exposure') rather than one blanket claim.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stating that both frequency and wavelength increase (or both decrease) together across the spectrum.
common_mistakes.why: Both are often described as simply 'changing' along the spectrum diagram, without checking which direction each one actually goes.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check any stated frequency-wavelength pair against c = fλ with a fixed c: if both increase together, the calculated speed could not stay fixed, which is impossible.

exam_notes: State explicitly that electromagnetic waves share the same speed only in vacuum (and approximately in air); do not generalise this to every medium.
When identifying a region from a calculated wavelength or frequency, give a reason that compares the calculated value's scale with that region's typical range, not just the region's name alone.
Pair any hazard statement with the specific region and the word 'excessive'; a general claim about danger without naming the region or the exposure level rarely earns credit.

summary.big_idea: Radio waves, visible light, X-rays and every other electromagnetic wave are the same fundamental kind of wave, all sharing one fixed speed in vacuum, ordered into seven regions by frequency and wavelength (which always vary oppositely), with hazard depending on the specific region, not on simply being electromagnetic.
key_points: The seven regions, in order of increasing frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
Every electromagnetic wave shares the same speed in a vacuum (c ≈ 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s), whatever its frequency or wavelength.
Frequency and wavelength vary in opposite directions across the spectrum, since their product equals the fixed speed c.

Excessive exposure to ultraviolet, X-ray or gamma radiation can damage cells; ordinary radio and microwave exposure is not associated with this, so hazard depends on the specific region, not on being 'electromagnetic' in general.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in vacuum; moving from radio to gamma, frequency rises and wavelength falls together, and hazard is specific to each region, not a blanket property of being 'electromagnetic'.

07_Sound_as_a_longitudinal_wave.json.title: Sound as a longitudinal wave
07_Sound_as_a_longitudinal_wave.json.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Explain that sound is produced by a vibrating source and needs a material medium to travel, describe how its speed can be measured, relate frequency to pitch and amplitude to loudness, calculate distances and times for echoes, and state that ultrasound has a frequency above 20 kHz.
Explain sound as a longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions, and state the general order of its speed in solids, liquids and gases.

prerequisites.statement: Describe a longitudinal wave as one whose vibration is parallel to its direction of travel, with frequency and amplitude as in the first lesson of this unit.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Sound is this unit's main real-world example of a longitudinal wave; every term introduced for it earlier (frequency, amplitude, compression, rarefaction) is reused directly here.

prerequisites.statement: Describe reflection as a wave bouncing back into the medium it came from.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: An echo is simply the reflection of sound off a surface; the speed-measurement method in this lesson depends on that reflected wave travelling back to a detector.

diagnostic_items.question: A long spring lies on a bench and a longitudinal wave travels along it from left to right. In which direction do the coils of the spring move as the wave passes, and do the coils themselves travel from one end of the spring to the other?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The coils vibrate left and right, backwards and forwards along the same line the wave travels, because in a longitudinal wave the vibration is parallel to the direction of travel. The coils themselves do not travel along the spring: each one oscillates about its own position while the wave, and the energy it carries, moves along.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Up and down, at right angles to the direction the wave travels.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is describing a transverse wave, so compressions and rarefactions have no reason to form and none of this lesson's sound diagrams can be read.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The coils travel along the spring from left to right with the wave.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner treats the wave as a flow of material rather than a travelling disturbance, which later turns a sound wave into a wind of moving air.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Compressions and rarefactions are simply the bunching and spreading that a vibration parallel to the travel direction produces; if that vibration is still pictured as side-to-side, or as matter being carried along, every explanation of sound in this lesson collapses.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Push one end of a spring sharply in and out and watch a single marked coil: it moves along the spring's own line and comes back, while the squeeze travels away from your hand. Then name the two directions separately - vibration direction and travel direction - for a longitudinal and for a transverse wave.

diagnostic_items.question: A wave travelling through air meets a hard flat wall and is reflected. State whether its speed and its wavelength are changed by the reflection, and explain your answer.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Neither is changed. The reflected wave travels back through the same medium, air, so its speed is the same; its frequency is still the frequency of the source, so from $v = f\lambda$ its wavelength is unchanged too. What usually does change is the amplitude, because the wall absorbs some of the energy.

common_wrong_answers.answer: It slows down, because it has bounced off the wall.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner expects a boundary always to change the speed; that happens when a wave crosses into a different medium, but a reflected wave never leaves the medium it started in.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The wavelength gets shorter, because the wave has lost energy.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner uses wavelength as a measure of the wave's energy, confusing it with amplitude, which is the quantity that falls when energy is absorbed.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: The echo method in this lesson assumes the reflected sound returns through the same air at the same speed, so that one value of $v$ serves for the whole round trip; a student who thinks reflection changes the speed cannot justify $v = 2d/t$.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Say what reflection means before using it: the wave turns round and carries on in the medium it came from. Then go through the quantities one at a time - speed unchanged, wavelength unchanged, direction reversed, amplitude possibly smaller.

theory_blocks.title: Vibration, pressure, and why sound needs a medium
theory_blocks.body:
Every sound starts with something vibrating: a tuning fork's prongs, a guitar string, your vocal cords. As the vibrating surface moves back and forth, it pushes and pulls on the air particles next to it, creating a travelling pattern of **compressions** (particles pushed closer together, higher pressure) and **rarefactions** (particles spread further apart, lower pressure). This pressure pattern is [[blue:sound: a longitudinal wave]], exactly as introduced earlier in this unit.

Because sound travels by particles pushing their neighbours, it needs particles to push: a material medium, solid, liquid or gas. With no particles present, as in a vacuum, there is nothing to carry the compressions and rarefactions along, so sound cannot travel through a vacuum at all. This is unlike light and the rest of the electromagnetic spectrum, which travels perfectly well through empty space.

theory_blocks.title: Pitch, loudness, and the limits of hearing
theory_blocks.body:
Two separate properties of a sound wave control how it is heard:

- **Frequency** controls **pitch**: a higher frequency sounds higher-pitched; a lower frequency sounds lower-pitched.
- **Amplitude** controls **loudness**: a larger amplitude sounds louder; a smaller amplitude sounds quieter.

These two properties are independent: changing one does not change the other. Normal human hearing covers roughly $20\,\mathrm{Hz}$ to $20\,\mathrm{kHz}$ ($20\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$). Sound above this range, with frequency greater than $20\,\mathrm{kHz}$, is called **ultrasound**: it is still an ordinary longitudinal sound wave, just at a frequency too high for human ears to detect.

assets.caption: Left: two sounds of equal amplitude but different frequency differ only in pitch. Right: two sounds of equal frequency but different amplitude differ only in loudness. The two properties change independently of each other.
assets.purpose: Make the independence of pitch (frequency) and loudness (amplitude) directly visible, targeting the related idea.

theory_blocks.title: Echoes and measuring the speed of sound
theory_blocks.body:
An **echo** is simply a reflection of sound off a surface, such as a cliff or a wall. If a sound is made at one point and reflects off a surface a distance $d$ away before returning to a detector at (or near) that same point, the sound has travelled a **round trip**: out to the surface, a distance $d$, and back again, a further distance $d$, a total of $2d$.

If the time for the whole round trip is $t$, and the speed of sound in the medium is $v$, then:
$$v = \dfrac{2d}{t} \qquad \text{or equivalently} \qquad d = \dfrac{vt}{2}$$
For example, with $v=340\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and a measured echo time of $t=0.50\,\mathrm{s}$, the reflecting surface is $d=(340\times0.50)/2=85\,\mathrm{m}$ away. This same round-trip idea, run in reverse, is how the speed of sound itself can be measured: time how long an echo takes to return from a surface at a known distance, then solve for $v$.

assets.caption: An echo's sound path: out to the reflecting surface (distance d) and back again (a further distance d), a round trip of 2d, covered in the measured time t. With v = 340 m/s and t = 0.50 s, d = (340×0.50)/2 = 85 m.
assets.purpose: Make the round-trip path explicit, directly targeting the related idea.

theory_blocks.title: Inside a sound wave: compressions and rarefactions
theory_blocks.body: Looking more closely at the particles of the medium as a sound wave passes through, each particle oscillates back and forth along the same line the wave travels, exactly as introduced for longitudinal waves earlier in this unit. This produces a repeating pattern: **compressions**, where particles are momentarily bunched closer together than normal (higher pressure), and **rarefactions**, where particles are momentarily spread further apart than normal (lower pressure). One full wavelength of sound is the distance from one compression to the next.

assets.caption: The source vibrates back and forth along the same line as the wave travels, which is what makes sound longitudinal. Each vibration sends out a compression, where the particles are bunched closer together, followed by a rarefaction, where they are spread further apart; one wavelength is the distance from one compression to the next.
assets.purpose: Give sound its own particle-level figure, reusing the verified compression/rarefaction spacing model.

theory_blocks.title: Why sound travels fastest in solids
theory_blocks.body:
The speed of sound depends on how quickly a disturbance can pass from one particle to the next, which in turn depends on how tightly and how stiffly the particles of the medium are bonded together. In general:
$$v_{\text{solid}} > v_{\text{liquid}} > v_{\text{gas}}$$
Particles in a solid are packed closely and held by strong, stiff bonds, so a push on one particle is transmitted to its neighbour almost immediately. Particles in a liquid are still close together but less rigidly bonded, giving a somewhat slower transmission. Particles in a gas are far apart and only interact through occasional collisions, giving the slowest transmission of the three states.

keywords.definition: A wave whose vibration is parallel to its direction of travel; sound is the standard example, with compressions and rarefactions instead of crests and troughs.
How high or low a sound is perceived to be, determined by its frequency.
How loud or quiet a sound is perceived to be, determined by its amplitude.
A reflection of sound off a surface, returning to a detector after travelling a round-trip distance.
Sound with a frequency above 20,000 Hz (20 kHz), beyond the upper limit of normal human hearing.

worked_examples.statement: **A simple echo.** A sound reflects off a cliff and returns to its source after $0.50\,\mathrm{s}$. The speed of sound in air is $340\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Calculate the distance to the cliff.
reasoning: The measured time covers the round trip (there and back), so use $d=vt/2$, not $d=vt$.
worked_examples.solution: $d = (340\times0.50)\div2 = 85\,\mathrm{m}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: the round-trip distance is $2\times85=170\,\mathrm{m}$, and $170\div340=0.50\,\mathrm{s}$, matching the given time.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Calculating $d=340\times0.50=170\,\mathrm{m}$, forgetting to divide by 2 for the round trip.

worked_examples.statement: **Finding the echo time.** A ship's sonar sends a sound pulse straight down to the sea floor, $450\,\mathrm{m}$ below. The speed of sound in seawater is $1500\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Calculate the time until the echo returns.
reasoning: Rearrange $d=vt/2$ to make $t$ the subject: $t=2d/v$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check: $d=vt/2=(1500\times0.60)\div2=450\,\mathrm{m}$, matching the given depth.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Calculating $t=d/v$ (the one-way time) instead of $t=2d/v$ (the round-trip time that an echo actually measures).

worked_examples.statement: **A one-way speed measurement.** Two students stand $680\,\mathrm{m}$ apart. One fires a starting pistol; the other starts a stopwatch on seeing the smoke and stops it on hearing the bang, measuring $2.0\,\mathrm{s}$. (a) Calculate the speed of sound from this data. (b) Explain why this calculation does not need a 'divide by 2' step, unlike an echo calculation.
reasoning: (a) This is a one-way measurement: the sound travels directly from the pistol to the listener, once.
(b) Compare this path with an echo's path.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $v = 680\div2.0 = 340\,\mathrm{m/s}$. (b) The sound here travels only once, directly from the pistol to the listener; it does not reflect off anything and come back, so the full measured distance (not half of it) corresponds to the full measured time.
worked_examples.interpretation: Contrasting this one-way method with the round-trip echo method in the previous examples reinforces exactly when a 'divide by 2' step is needed and when it is not.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Automatically halving the distance or doubling the time out of habit from echo problems, when this particular setup is not an echo at all.

worked_examples.statement: **Pitch, loudness and ultrasound together.** A loudspeaker produces sound A at $500\,\mathrm{Hz}$ with a large amplitude, and sound B at $2000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ with a small amplitude. A separate device produces a signal at $45\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$. (a) State which of sound A and B is louder, and which has the higher pitch. (b) State whether the $45\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ signal is audible to humans, and name this type of signal if not.
unknowns: audibility of the 45,000 Hz signal (part b)
reasoning: (a) Loudness depends on amplitude; pitch depends on frequency. These are judged independently.
(b) Compare $45\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ with the upper limit of human hearing, $20\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$.
worked_examples.solution: (a) Sound A is louder (larger amplitude); sound B has the higher pitch (higher frequency). (b) $45\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ exceeds $20\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$, so it is not audible to humans; it is ultrasound.
worked_examples.interpretation: The result follows from the scientific principle used in the solution and shows how to apply that principle when the context or data change.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Calling sound A 'higher-pitched' because it is louder, conflating amplitude with frequency.

guided_exercises.statement: A ship's horn echoes off a cliff. The speed of sound is $330\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and the echo returns after $0.60\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the distance to the cliff.
hints: Decide whether the measured time is one-way or round-trip.
Use $d=vt/2$ for a round-trip echo time.
Check your answer by doubling it and comparing with $vt$.
common_errors: Forgetting to divide by 2 and reporting $198\,\mathrm{m}$.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Decide whether the measured time is one-way or round-trip.

**Step 2 — Method:** Use $d=vt/2$ for a round-trip echo time.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $d = (330\times0.60)\div2 = 99\,\mathrm{m}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your answer by doubling it and comparing with $vt$.

guided_exercises.statement: Sound X has a low frequency and a small amplitude. Sound Y has a high frequency and a large amplitude. State which sound is louder, and which has the higher pitch.
hints: Loudness depends only on amplitude.
Pitch depends only on frequency.
Compare each property separately; do not assume they must agree.
guided_exercises.answer: Sound Y is louder (larger amplitude) and also has the higher pitch (higher frequency).
common_errors: Assuming the two sounds must differ in only one property at a time, when a real comparison can differ in both.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Loudness depends only on amplitude.

**Step 2 — Method:** Pitch depends only on frequency.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Sound Y is louder (larger amplitude) and also has the higher pitch (higher frequency).

**Step 4 — Check:** Compare each property separately; do not assume they must agree.

exercises.statement: A sound echoes off a wall and returns after $0.80\,\mathrm{s}$. The speed of sound is $340\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Calculate the distance to the wall.
exercises.full_solution: Check: round trip $=2\times136=272\,\mathrm{m}$; $272\div340=0.80\,\mathrm{s}$, matching the given time.

exercises.statement: Explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum, while light (and the rest of the electromagnetic spectrum) can.
exercises.answer: Sound travels by particles of a medium colliding with and pushing their neighbours; with no particles present in a vacuum, there is nothing to carry the compressions and rarefactions along, so sound cannot travel through it. Light and other electromagnetic waves do not need a medium at all, and can travel through empty space.
exercises.full_solution: This contrasts sound's mechanical, particle-to-particle transmission with the electromagnetic spectrum's ability to travel without any medium, covered earlier in this unit.

exercises.statement: A signal has a frequency of $45\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$. State the normal range of human hearing, and state whether this signal is audible or classed as ultrasound.
exercises.answer: Normal human hearing covers roughly $20\,\mathrm{Hz}$ to $20\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$. Since $45\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ is above $20\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$, it is not audible; it is classed as ultrasound.
exercises.full_solution: Comparing directly against the $20\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ upper limit is the whole method here.

exercises.statement: A person can sometimes hear an approaching train by putting an ear to the rail before the sound becomes audible through the air. Using the general speed order of sound in different states of matter, explain this observation.
exercises.answer: Sound travels fastest in solids, then liquids, then gases, because particles in a solid are packed closely and bonded stiffly, transmitting a disturbance to their neighbours almost immediately. The steel rail is a solid, so sound (vibration) from the approaching train reaches the listener's ear through the rail considerably faster than the same sound travelling to them through the air, which is why it can be heard there first.
exercises.full_solution: Sound travels fastest in solids, then liquids, then gases, because particles in a solid are packed closely and bonded stiffly, transmitting a disturbance to their neighbours almost immediately. The steel rail is a solid, so sound (vibration) from the approaching train reaches the listener's ear through the rail considerably faster than the same sound travelling to them through the air, which is why it can be heard there first.

exam_questions.statement: A submarine sends a sound pulse towards the sea floor directly below it. The speed of sound in seawater is $1500\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and the echo returns after $1.0\,\mathrm{s}$. (a) Calculate the depth of the sea floor below the submarine. (b) A second pulse, sent later, takes $1.4\,\mathrm{s}$ to return. State, with a reason, whether the sea floor at this new position is deeper or shallower than before.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $d=(1500\times1.0)\div2=750\,\mathrm{m}$. (b) Deeper: a longer echo time means a longer round-trip distance (since speed is unchanged), so the sea floor is further away, meaning deeper.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $d=(1500\times1.0)\div2=750\,\mathrm{m}$. (b) Deeper: a longer echo time means a longer round-trip distance (since speed is unchanged), so the sea floor is further away, meaning deeper.
mark_scheme: Calculates $d=750\,\mathrm{m}$ for part (a).
States the sea floor is deeper for part (b).
Gives a reason linking longer time to greater distance with v unchanged.
Shows the round-trip halving in part (a): $d=(1500\times1.0)\div2$ (method mark).
common_errors: Forgetting to divide by 2 in part (a), giving $1500\,\mathrm{m}$ instead of $750\,\mathrm{m}$.

exam_questions.statement: A sound engineer increases a sound's amplitude without changing its frequency, and separately records a second sound of higher frequency but identical amplitude to the original. (a) Describe the change heard in each case. (b) The engineer also produces a $15\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ tone and a $25\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ tone. State which, if either, is inaudible to a person with normal hearing, with a reason.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Increasing amplitude alone makes the sound louder, with no change in pitch. Increasing frequency alone (at the same amplitude) makes the sound higher-pitched, with no change in loudness. (b) The $25\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ tone is inaudible, because it exceeds the upper limit of human hearing ($20\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$); the $15\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ tone is within the normal hearing range and would be audible.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) Increasing amplitude alone makes the sound louder, with no change in pitch. Increasing frequency alone (at the same amplitude) makes the sound higher-pitched, with no change in loudness. (b) The $25\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ tone is inaudible, because it exceeds the upper limit of human hearing ($20\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$); the $15\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ tone is within the normal hearing range and would be audible.
mark_scheme: States that increased amplitude alone gives a louder sound, same pitch.
States that increased frequency alone gives a higher pitch, same loudness.
Identifies $25\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ as inaudible (ultrasound).
Identifies $15\,000\,\mathrm{Hz}$ as audible, with a correct reason referencing the 20,000 Hz limit.
common_errors: Stating that increasing amplitude changes the pitch, when only the frequency change in the second sound affects pitch.

challenge_questions.statement: A survey ship sends a short pulse of ultrasound of frequency $50\,\mathrm{kHz}$ straight down from its hull and receives the reflection from the sea bed $0.090\,\mathrm{s}$ later. The speed of sound in sea water is $1500\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and in air it is $340\,\mathrm{m/s}$. (a) Calculate the depth of the sea bed below the hull. (b) Explain why nobody on board hears the pulse. (c) Calculate the wavelength of the pulse in the sea water, and the wavelength the same transmitter would produce in air. (d) Explain, in terms of particles, why the speed of sound in sea water is so much greater than in air.
hints: The pulse makes a round trip: down to the sea bed and back again.
For part (b), compare the frequency with the upper limit of normal human hearing.
In part (c) the transmitter fixes the frequency, not the wavelength, so use $v = f\lambda$ separately in each medium.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) The pulse covers twice the depth, so $d = vt/2 = (1500\times0.090)/2 = 67.5\,\mathrm{m}$. (b) The frequency is $50\,\mathrm{kHz}$, which is above the $20\,\mathrm{kHz}$ upper limit of normal human hearing, so the pulse is ultrasound and human ears cannot detect it. (c) In sea water $\lambda = v/f = 1500/50\,000 = 0.030\,\mathrm{m}$, that is 3.0 cm. The transmitter still vibrates $50\,000$ times a second whatever it is in, so in air $\lambda = 340/50\,000 = 6.8\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$, that is 6.8 mm: the same frequency gives a much shorter wavelength where the speed is lower. (d) Sound travels by each particle pushing its neighbours. In water the particles are close together and interact strongly and continuously, so a compression is passed on almost at once. In air the particles are far apart and pass the disturbance on only through occasional collisions, so it travels much more slowly. In general sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases.
challenge_questions.full_solution: (a) The pulse covers twice the depth, so $d = vt/2 = (1500\times0.090)/2 = 67.5\,\mathrm{m}$. (b) The frequency is $50\,\mathrm{kHz}$, which is above the $20\,\mathrm{kHz}$ upper limit of normal human hearing, so the pulse is ultrasound and human ears cannot detect it. (c) In sea water $\lambda = v/f = 1500/50\,000 = 0.030\,\mathrm{m}$, that is 3.0 cm. The transmitter still vibrates $50\,000$ times a second whatever it is in, so in air $\lambda = 340/50\,000 = 6.8\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$, that is 6.8 mm: the same frequency gives a much shorter wavelength where the speed is lower. (d) Sound travels by each particle pushing its neighbours. In water the particles are close together and interact strongly and continuously, so a compression is passed on almost at once. In air the particles are far apart and pass the disturbance on only through occasional collisions, so it travels much more slowly. In general sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases.

mcq.stem: An astronaut on a planet with no atmosphere sets off a small explosion. Would a second astronaut standing nearby, outside any spacecraft, hear it?

options.text: No, because sound needs a material medium to travel through, and there is no atmosphere to carry it.
Yes, because sound, like light, can travel through a vacuum.
options.why_wrong: wrongly treats sound the same as light; sound specifically cannot travel through a vacuum.

options.text: Yes, but only very faintly, because a little sound always leaks through a vacuum.
options.why_wrong: invents a partial transmission through a vacuum that does not occur for a mechanical wave like sound.

options.text: No, but only because the explosion itself would be too quiet to hear, not because of the vacuum.
options.why_wrong: misses the actual reason (no medium to carry the sound) and substitutes an unrelated one.

mcq.explanation: Sound travels by particles pushing their neighbours; with no atmosphere (no medium), there is nothing to carry the compressions and rarefactions, so sound cannot be heard there.

mcq.stem: A sound's amplitude is increased while its frequency stays exactly the same. What change, if any, would be heard?

options.text: The sound becomes higher-pitched; its loudness stays the same.
options.why_wrong: wrongly links amplitude with pitch; pitch is set by frequency, which has not changed here.

options.text: The sound becomes louder; its pitch stays the same.
The sound becomes both louder and higher-pitched.
options.why_wrong: wrongly assumes loudness and pitch must change together; only amplitude changed, so only loudness changes.

options.text: Nothing would be heard to change, since frequency is unchanged.
options.why_wrong: ignores that loudness, which depends on amplitude, would still change even with frequency fixed.

mcq.explanation: Amplitude controls loudness; with frequency unchanged, pitch does not change, but the increased amplitude makes the sound louder.

mcq.stem: A sound echoes off a cliff $120\,\mathrm{m}$ away. The speed of sound is $340\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is the correct method to find the time for the echo to return?

options.text: $t = 120\div340$, because the sound only travels the distance to the cliff.
options.why_wrong: uses only the one-way distance, ignoring that an echo requires the sound to also travel back.

options.text: $t = 120\times340$, multiplying the distance and speed together.
options.why_wrong: multiplies distance by speed instead of dividing distance by speed, giving a result with the wrong units entirely.

options.text: $t = (2\times120)\div340$, because the sound travels to the cliff and back.
$t = 340\div120$, dividing speed by distance.
options.why_wrong: inverts the correct division, giving a frequency-like quantity rather than a time.

mcq.explanation: An echo is a round trip: the sound travels $120\,\mathrm{m}$ out and $120\,\mathrm{m}$ back, a total of $240\,\mathrm{m}$, so $t=240\div340$, which is the same as $(2\times120)\div340$.

mcq.stem: Which lists the speed of sound correctly, from fastest to slowest?

options.text: Gas, liquid, solid.
options.why_wrong: reverses the correct order completely: gases give the slowest transmission, not the fastest.

options.text: Liquid, solid, gas.
options.why_wrong: places liquid above solid, when a solid's closely packed, stiffly bonded particles transmit sound fastest.

options.text: All three are exactly the same speed, since sound is sound regardless of the medium.
options.why_wrong: ignores that the medium's particle spacing and bonding directly affects how quickly a disturbance is transmitted.

options.text: Solid, liquid, gas.

mcq.explanation: Sound travels fastest in solids (closely packed, stiffly bonded particles), then liquids, then slowest in gases (widely spaced particles, infrequent collisions).

flashcards.front: Why does sound need a medium to travel, unlike light?
flashcards.back: Sound travels by particles colliding with and pushing their neighbours; with no particles (a vacuum), there is nothing to carry it. Light does not need a medium.

flashcards.front: State the echo/speed-of-sound relation, and explain the 2.
flashcards.back: v = 2d/t (or d = vt/2): the 2 accounts for the round trip, out to the reflecting surface and back again.

flashcards.front: Does a larger amplitude make a sound higher-pitched?
flashcards.back: No. Amplitude controls loudness; frequency controls pitch. The two are independent.

flashcards.front: Compare the speed of sound in solids, liquids and gases.
flashcards.back: Fastest in solids (closely packed, stiffly bonded particles), slower in liquids, slowest in gases (widely spaced particles).

flashcards.front: What is ultrasound, and how does it relate to human hearing?
flashcards.back: Sound with frequency above 20,000 Hz (20 kHz); above the upper limit of normal human hearing (roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz), so it is inaudible to humans.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Sound can travel through a vacuum, just like light.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Light and sound are both commonly called 'waves' and both travel through air every day, which can suggest they behave the same way in every situation, including a vacuum.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts that sound from an explosion in space could be heard, or that a bell in an evacuated jar would ring as loudly as in air.
misconceptions.correct_model: Sound is a mechanical (pressure) wave: it travels by particles of the medium colliding with and pushing their neighbours, passing the disturbance along. With no particles present, as in a vacuum, there is nothing to transmit the compressions and rarefactions, so sound cannot travel through a vacuum. Electromagnetic waves, unlike sound, do not need a medium and can cross a vacuum.
misconceptions.remediation: Picture a ringing bell inside a jar as air is pumped out: the sound fades as the particles that would carry it are removed, even though the bell keeps vibrating and can still be seen.
related_exercises: the vacuum-versus-light comparison exercise in this lesson

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A larger amplitude means a higher pitch.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: 'Bigger' and 'higher' both sound like they should describe the same kind of increase, so a bigger wave can be assumed to sound higher-pitched rather than simply louder.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a louder sound as also being higher-pitched, without any change having been made to its frequency.
misconceptions.correct_model: Amplitude relates to loudness, not pitch: a larger amplitude gives a louder sound, at whatever pitch it already had. Pitch is set by frequency: a higher frequency gives a higher pitch, completely independent of amplitude.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare two sounds that differ only in amplitude (same note, played quietly and loudly) with two sounds that differ only in frequency (two different notes at the same volume), to show loudness and pitch change independently.
related_exercises: the pitch/loudness comparison diagram in this lesson's theory

misconceptions.incorrect_model: An echo's sound only travels the one-way distance to the reflecting surface, not there and back.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The measured time is for 'the sound coming back', which can be read as only covering the return leg, rather than the whole round trip.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner calculates a reflecting surface's distance as speed × time, without dividing by two.
misconceptions.correct_model: In an echo, sound travels from its starting point to the reflecting surface, then back again to the listener: a full round trip. The measured time covers this whole round trip, so the one-way distance to the surface is half of (speed × time), not the full value.
misconceptions.remediation: Sketch the sound's path as two separate, equal legs (source to surface, then surface to listener) before writing any equation, so the round trip is visible, not assumed.
related_exercises: every echo calculation in this lesson

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating sound as able to travel through a vacuum, by analogy with light.
common_mistakes.why: Both are commonly called 'waves' and both travel through air every day, which blurs the distinction between them.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember sound is a mechanical, particle-to-particle wave: no particles (a vacuum) means no sound. Light needs no medium at all.

common_mistakes.mistake: Linking a larger amplitude with a higher pitch.
common_mistakes.why: 'Bigger' and 'higher' can both sound like the same kind of increase in everyday language.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Keep amplitude -> loudness and frequency -> pitch as two separate, independent pairings; never let one imply a change in the other.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calculating an echo distance as speed × time, without dividing by 2.
common_mistakes.why: The measured time is for 'the sound returning', which can be misread as the one-way travel time.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Sketch the sound's path as two equal legs (out and back) before writing any equation, to make the round trip visible.

exam_notes: State explicitly that an echo calculation uses the round-trip distance or time; writing the divide-by-2 step out, rather than skipping straight to a final answer, is often credited separately.
Keep loudness (amplitude) and pitch (frequency) answered as two separate statements, even when a question describes both properties changing at once.
Give the 20,000 Hz boundary explicitly when classifying a frequency as audible or ultrasound, not just a verbal description.

summary.big_idea: Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave, produced by a vibrating source, that needs a material medium to travel, with frequency controlling pitch, amplitude controlling loudness, and echoes revealing distance through a round-trip speed calculation.
key_points: Sound needs a material medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel; it cannot travel through a vacuum, unlike light.
Frequency determines pitch; amplitude determines loudness; the two change independently of each other.
An echo's measured time covers a round trip (there and back), so distance = speed × time ÷ 2.
Human hearing covers roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz; sound above 20 kHz is ultrasound. Sound travels fastest in solids, then liquids, then slowest in gases.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Sound needs a medium and cannot cross a vacuum; frequency sets pitch and amplitude sets loudness, independently; and any echo calculation needs its round-trip divide-by-2.

summary.big_idea: Use the key physics ideas and methods from waves light and sound accurately in mixed practice and exam-style problems.

exercises.statement: the supplied diagram shows the crests of straight ripples in a ripple tank, moving to the right. Six consecutive crests are labelled, in order, F, E, D, C, B, A (A being the leading crest, furthest in the direction of travel), and the total distance from crest F to crest A is 5 cm. (a) What is the wavelength of the ripples? (b) If 5 seconds ago ripple A occupied the position now occupied by ripple F, what is the frequency of the ripples? (c) What is the speed of the ripples?
exercises.full_solution: (a) The 5 cm shown in the figure spans the six crests F to A, i.e. 5 equal gaps between consecutive crests, so one wavelength is 5 cm ÷ 5 = 1 cm.
