(b) Saying '5 seconds ago ripple A occupied the position now occupied by ripple F' means a single crest has travelled the whole distance from F's position to A's position (5 cm = 5 wavelengths) in 5 s. So one wavelength passes a fixed point every 5 s ÷ 5 = 1 s, and frequency f = 1/T = 1/(1 s) = 1 Hz. (c) By the wave equation v = fλ: v = 1 Hz × 1 cm = 1 cm/s. Check: distance/time = 5 cm/5 s = 1 cm/s, which agrees with the wave-equation answer (= 0.01 m/s).
exercises.source_label: P4 Properties of Waves, 'Diffraction' section Questions, Q1 (Figure P4.11)

exercises.statement: During the refraction of a wave, which two of the following properties change? A The speed. B The frequency. C The wavelength.
exercises.answer: A and C (the speed and the wavelength both change; the frequency does not change).
exercises.full_solution: Refraction happens precisely because a wave's speed changes when it crosses into a new medium. The frequency of a wave is fixed by its source and is unaffected by the medium it is travelling through, so it stays the same on both sides of the boundary. Since v = fλ and f is constant, a change in speed v must be matched by a proportional change in wavelength λ. So the two properties that change are the speed (A) and the wavelength (C); the frequency (B) is unchanged.
exercises.source_label: P4 Properties of Waves, 'Diffraction' section Questions, Q2

exercises.statement: One side of a ripple tank ABCD is raised slightly (the supplied diagram), and a ripple is started at a point P near the centre of the tank with a finger. After 1 second the ripple is not a circle but an oval, having spread noticeably further towards the DC edge of the tank than towards the AB edge in that same time. (a) Why is the ripple not circular? (b) Which side of the tank (AB or DC) has been raised?
exercises.answer: (a) Because the wave travels at different speeds in different parts of the tank, since the water depth is not uniform. (b) The AB side has been raised.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Ripples (water waves) travel faster in deeper water and more slowly in shallow water. Raising one side of the tank makes the water above it shallower, so a wavefront heading towards that side slows down, while a wavefront heading towards the opposite, still-deep side keeps travelling at its normal (faster) speed. Since the wave does not cover the same distance in every direction in the same time, the wavefront spreads out into a 'squashed' oval rather than a circle. (b) Measuring the figure, the oval is centred almost on the vertical line through P but is stretched much further towards the DC edge than towards the AB edge, meaning the wave travelled a shorter distance (i.e. moved more slowly) towards AB in the same 1 second. Because wave speed is lower in shallower water, the AB side must be the one that was raised.
exercises.source_label: P4 Properties of Waves, 'Diffraction' section Questions, Q3 (Figure P4.12)

exercises.statement: In the 'Refraction in glass' experiment (the supplied diagram), a ray of light from a lamp passes through a single slit and strikes a rectangular glass block ABCD lying on a sheet of paper, hitting face AB. What two things happen to the light falling on AB?
exercises.answer: Part of the light is reflected off the surface AB, and part of it is refracted (bent) as it passes into the glass.
exercises.full_solution: Whenever light reaches the boundary between two different transparent media (here, air and glass), that boundary is only partly transparent to it. Some of the light is reflected back into the air (a faint reflected ray can be seen bouncing off AB), while the rest of the light crosses into the glass, changing direction as it does so (bending towards the normal, because glass is optically denser than air) — this bending is refraction. So both partial reflection and refraction occur at AB at the same time.
exercises.source_label: P4 Properties of Waves, 'Practical work: Refraction in glass' Questions, Q1 (Figure P4.20)

exercises.statement: (a) When the ray enters the glass block at AB (the supplied diagram), is it bent towards or away from the part of the normal that lies inside the block? (b) How is the ray bent as it leaves the block at CD?
exercises.answer: (a) Towards the normal. (b) Away from the normal.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Glass is optically denser than air, and a ray entering an optically denser medium at an angle is always bent towards the normal — from the refraction rule stated above. (b) At CD the ray is leaving the glass and re-entering air, which is optically less dense than glass, so here it is bent away from the normal instead.
exercises.source_label: P4 Properties of Waves, 'Practical work: Refraction in glass' Questions, Q2 (Figure P4.20)

exercises.statement: What can you say about the direction of the ray falling on AB and the direction of the ray leaving CD (the supplied diagram)?
exercises.answer: They travel in the same (parallel) direction — the emerging ray is simply shifted sideways compared with the ray that entered.
exercises.full_solution: Faces AB and CD of the block are parallel to one another. The ray bends towards the normal by a certain angle on entering at AB, then, on reaching the parallel face CD, it bends away from the normal by exactly the same angle, which undoes the first bend. So the ray leaving CD ends up travelling in exactly the same direction as the ray that struck AB — it has only been displaced sideways (laterally) by its path through the glass, not rotated.
exercises.source_label: P4 Properties of Waves, 'Practical work: Refraction in glass' Questions, Q3 (Figure P4.20)

exercises.statement: What happens if the ray hits face AB at right angles (i.e. travelling along the normal)?
exercises.answer: It is not refracted at all — it carries straight on through the glass undeviated.
exercises.full_solution: A ray travelling exactly along the normal direction meets the boundary with an angle of incidence of 0°. Refraction only changes the direction of a ray that crosses a boundary at a non-zero angle to the normal; a ray along the normal has no sideways component to bend, so it passes straight through both surfaces of the block without changing direction (though it still slows down and speeds up again inside the glass).
exercises.source_label: P4 Properties of Waves, 'Practical work: Refraction in glass' Questions, Q4 (Figure P4.20)

exercises.statement: the supplied diagram shows a ray of light PQ striking a mirror AB at point Q, where the angle between mirror AB and the incoming ray QP is 50°. Mirror AB and mirror CD meet each other at a right angle (90°). QN is the normal to mirror AB at Q. (a) What is the angle of incidence of ray PQ on mirror AB? (b) Describe (in words) the path the ray PQ takes after it has reflected off both mirrors. (c) What are the values of the angle of reflection at AB, the angle of incidence at CD, and the angle of reflection at CD? (d) What do you notice about the path of the ray PQ and the path of the final reflected ray?
exercises.answer: (a) 40°. (b) The ray reflects off AB at Q, crosses to mirror CD, reflects off CD and travels back out of the corner, heading back towards the side it came from. (c) Angle of reflection at AB = 40°; angle of incidence at CD = 50°; angle of reflection at CD = 50°. (d) The final ray travels parallel to the original ray PQ, but in the exact opposite direction (it is displaced sideways).
exercises.full_solution: (a) The normal QN is perpendicular to the mirror AB, so the angle between the mirror and the normal is 90°. The diagram gives the angle between the mirror AB and the incoming ray QP as 50°, so the angle between the ray and the normal (the angle of incidence) is 90° − 50° = 40°. (b)/(c) By the law of reflection, the angle of reflection at AB is also 40°, so the reflected ray leaves AB at 90° − 40° = 50° to the mirror surface and travels across to mirror CD. The reflected ray and the two mirrors form a triangle; its angles are 50° (between the ray and AB), 90° (where the mirrors meet) and therefore 180° − 90° − 50° = 40° between the ray and CD. The angle of incidence at CD is measured from the normal, so it is 90° − 40° = 50°, and by the law of reflection the angle of reflection at CD is also 50°. The ray then travels back out of the corner. (d) At AB the ray turns through 180° − 2 × 40° = 100°, and at CD it turns through 180° − 2 × 50° = 80°; in total it turns through 100° + 80° = 180°. So the final ray travels parallel to PQ but in the exact opposite direction, only displaced sideways. This is the 'corner reflector' property of two mirrors at right angles: whatever the angle of incidence, the ray is sent straight back the way it came (the idea behind bicycle reflectors and cat's-eyes).
exercises.source_label: P4 Properties of Waves, Questions, Q5 (Figure P4.31)

exercises.statement: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 60°, is reflected from the mirror and then strikes a second plane mirror placed so that the angle between the two mirrors is 45°. What is the angle of reflection at the second mirror? A 15° B 25° C 45° D 65° E 75°
exercises.full_solution: The angle of incidence at the first mirror is 60°, so the ray leaves the first mirror at 90° − 60° = 30° to its surface (angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 60° from the normal). The reflected ray then travels to the second mirror. The two mirrors and this ray form a triangle with angles 30° (between the ray and the first mirror) and 45° (between the mirrors), so the third angle, between the ray and the second mirror, is 180° − 30° − 45° = 105°. The acute angle between the ray and the second mirror is therefore 180° − 105° = 75°, and the angle of incidence (measured from the normal) is 90° − 75° = 15°. Since the angle of reflection always equals the angle of incidence, the angle of reflection at the second mirror is 15°, option A. (Drawing an accurate scale diagram with a protractor gives the same result.)
exercises.source_label: P4 Properties of Waves, Questions, Q6

exercises.statement: the supplied diagram shows a plane mirror lying along a horizontal line, with two points, E and D, marked on the mirror surface itself, and three further points, A, B and C, marked above the mirror. An observer's eye is positioned below the mirror on the left, and an object is positioned below the mirror, roughly directly beneath point D. At which of the points A to E will the observer see the image of the object in the mirror?
exercises.answer: B.
exercises.full_solution: A plane mirror forms a virtual image of an object as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it, measured along the perpendicular from the object to the mirror plane — and this image position depends only on the object and the mirror, not on where the observer's eye is. Measuring the positions in the figure, the object sits directly below point D, at a certain perpendicular distance below the mirror line. Reflecting that point across the mirror line (keeping the same horizontal position, at an equal distance on the far side) lands almost exactly on point B: point A is at the wrong horizontal position altogether (off to one side), and point C, although above the object's horizontal position, is far too close to the mirror to be the correct image distance. So the observer sees the image of the object at point B.
exercises.source_label: P4 Properties of Waves, Questions, Q7 (Figure P4.32)

exercises.statement: If 5 seconds elapse between a lightning flash and the clap of thunder, how far away is the storm? (Speed of sound = 330 m/s.)
exercises.full_solution: Light from the flash reaches an observer almost instantly, so essentially all of the 5 s delay is the time taken for the sound of the thunder to travel from the storm to the observer. Using distance = speed × time: d = 330 m/s × 5 s = 1650 m.
exercises.source_label: P4 Properties of Waves, Questions, Q23

exercises.statement: (a) A girl stands 160 m away from a high wall and claps her hands at a steady rate so that each clap coincides with the echo of the one before. If her clapping rate is 60 per minute, what value does this give for the speed of sound? (b) If she moves 40 m closer to the wall she finds the clapping rate has to be 80 per minute for each clap to again coincide with the echo of the previous one. What value do these new measurements give for the speed of sound? (c) If she moves again and finds the clapping rate becomes 30 per minute, how far is she from the wall, if the speed of sound is the value you found in (a)?
exercises.full_solution: (a) A clapping rate of 60 per minute means one clap every 60 s ÷ 60 = 1 s. Because each clap coincides with the echo of the previous one, the round-trip travel time of the sound (girl to wall and back, 2 × 160 m = 320 m) must equal this 1 s interval. So speed = distance/time = 320 m ÷ 1 s = 320 m/s. (b) Now the distance to the wall is 160 m − 40 m = 120 m, so the round trip is 2 × 120 m = 240 m. A rate of 80 claps per minute gives an interval of 60 s ÷ 80 = 0.75 s. Speed = 240 m ÷ 0.75 s = 320 m/s — the same value as in (a), which is a good consistency check on the method. (c) A rate of 30 claps per minute gives an interval of 60 s ÷ 30 = 2 s. Using the speed found in (a), 320 m/s, the round-trip distance is 320 m/s × 2 s = 640 m, so the one-way distance to the wall is 640 m ÷ 2 = 320 m.
exercises.source_label: P4 Properties of Waves, Questions, Q24

exercises.statement: (a) What properties of sound suggest that it is a wave motion? (b) How does a progressive transverse wave differ from a progressive longitudinal wave? Which type of wave is a sound wave?
exercises.answer: (a) Sound shows reflection (echoes), refraction and diffraction, and it transfers energy from source to listener without any net transfer of matter — all typical wave behaviours. (b) In a transverse wave the vibrations are at right angles to the direction of travel; in a longitudinal wave the vibrations are along (parallel to) the direction of travel, producing compressions and rarefactions. Sound is a longitudinal wave.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Sound can be reflected (producing echoes), refracted (its speed and direction change when it passes between regions of different temperature or density), and diffracted (it bends around corners and through doorways, which is why a sound can be heard from round a corner); it also carries energy from a source to a listener's ear without the air itself moving from one place to the other. All of these behaviours are characteristic of waves in general, which is why sound is classed as a wave motion rather than, say, a stream of particles travelling directly from source to listener. (b) In a progressive transverse wave the particles (or field quantities) vibrate at right angles to the direction the wave's energy travels — as on a vibrating rope or a water wave. In a progressive longitudinal wave the particles vibrate back and forth along the very same line as the direction of travel, which bunches particles together into compressions and spreads them apart into rarefactions, as on a pushed-and-pulled slinky spring. Sound in air is a longitudinal wave: air molecules vibrate back and forth along the direction the sound travels, creating a travelling pattern of compressions and rarefactions in air pressure/density.
exercises.source_label: P4 Properties of Waves, Questions, Q25

exercises.statement: (a) Sketch the waveform (a displacement–time graph) of: (i) a loud, low-pitched note; (ii) a soft, high-pitched note. (b) If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, what is the wavelength of a note of frequency: (i) 340 Hz; (ii) 170 Hz?
exercises.answer: (a)(i) Large amplitude, low frequency (widely spaced oscillations). (ii) Small amplitude, high frequency (closely spaced oscillations). (b)(i) 1 m. (ii) 2 m.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Loudness of a note is controlled by its amplitude, and pitch by its frequency. (i) A loud note has a large amplitude (tall peaks and troughs on the graph); a low-pitched note has a low frequency, so its oscillations are spaced far apart along the time axis (long period). This waveform should therefore be sketched with large, widely-spaced humps. (ii) A soft note has a small amplitude (short peaks and troughs); a high-pitched note has a high frequency, so its oscillations are packed closely together along the time axis (short period). This waveform should be sketched with small, closely-spaced humps. (b) Rearranging the wave equation v = fλ gives λ = v/f. (i) λ = 340 m/s ÷ 340 Hz = 1 m. (ii) λ = 340 m/s ÷ 170 Hz = 2 m (exactly double the wavelength of (i), as expected since its frequency is exactly half).
exercises.source_label: P4 Properties of Waves, Questions, Q26
